title: Rare Handshake: Russia and Germany Meet at the U.N.
summary: Two top diplomats from countries that don't get along just met face-to-face — and shook hands. On Saturday, German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov met on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. It's believed to be their first such meeting since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The meeting lasted about 20 minutes and was requested by Germany. Wadephul asked Russia to abandon its "dangerous path of escalation" toward Germany, Europe and NATO (a military alliance of countries including the U.S. and Germany). Lavrov was not impressed. He later told the U.N. that Germany is Ukraine's main sponsor and wants to be a military power in Europe. He even asked, "Didn't they not learn the lessons of World War II?" Lavrov also said Russia will block any attempt by Germany or Japan to get a permanent seat on the U.N. Security Council — the U.N.'s most powerful group. After the meeting, Lavrov said "nothing new" came from it. The two countries have been arguing more lately, especially after an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in Germany last month, which Germany blames on Russia.
why_it_matters: It shows that even countries that strongly disagree can still sit down and talk, and talking is one way to keep a big fight from getting worse for everyone.

background_read: The United Nations (a group where almost every country in the world meets to talk about big problems) holds a big meeting in New York every year, and leaders give speeches there.
NATO is a military alliance — a club of countries, including the U.S. and Germany, that promise to help defend each other if one is attacked.
The U.N. Security Council is the U.N.'s most powerful group; five countries — the U.S., Britain, France, Russia and China — have permanent seats and can block decisions.

perspectives.description: Some people see the handshake as a small but important sign that Russia and Germany are still willing to talk instead of fighting.
Russia's Sergey Lavrov said 'nothing new' came from the meeting, so others think the handshake changed nothing at all.
Experts say each side mostly repeated its own position: Germany asked Russia to stop escalating, and Russia blamed Germany for being Ukraine's main sponsor.
